payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
On Provenance

Two papers, two long-form essays, and a running series of notes, all working the same argument. This page is the body of work rather than the case for it. The case is made on the page that maps the whole thing, in about four minutes, and it is the better place to land if you arrived here cold. What follows is what has been argued so far, the conditions under which it would be wrong, and the things it does not claim.

The argument in three moves

There are three because each move only becomes necessary once the one before it holds, which is what the numbering on the essays has been asserting quietly and never saying out loud.

One, who made it

SSRN 6402298. The formal version carries the cost model and the citations; this is the argument without them.

Provenance Over Detection argues that detecting AI-generated music is the wrong instrument for the question the industry is actually asking. Detection is probabilistic, contestable, and degrades as generative models improve, so its accuracy is a function of a race it is structurally set up to lose. A signature captured at the moment of creation does not degrade. It resolves or it does not.

The paper also names the incentive problem underneath the market: a detection vendor's business grows with the problem it sells against, which is a poor foundation for infrastructure the industry has to trust for decades. No conspiracy is required for that to bite. It is what happens whenever the party selling the measurement is paid by the volume of what it measures.

Two, what identifies it

ISRC identifies a recording; ISWC identifies the underlying composition. Both are issued by institutions after a work is finished, which is the gap this argument works in.

Authorship verification alone was not enough, and that is the reason a second paper exists. Knowing a human made a recording does nothing for the person who has to route the money, because the systems that pay can only pay a name they are able to resolve. ISRC and ISWC are assigned by institutions, after the fact, to releases rather than to contributions, and everything they fail to match accumulates in an unmatched pool that nobody is in a hurry to drain.

Provenance as Substrate extends the framework into that identifier layer, treating the cryptographic record as the substrate the rights infrastructure sits on rather than a label attached to it. SSRN abstract 6730343, and in submission at the Journal of the Audio Engineering Society.

Three, who vouches for it

Both papers rest on an assumption neither of them argues: that a contributor's identity can be vouched for by somebody. For an artist inside an institution the assumption is invisible, because a label, a PRO, or a distributor already answers it. For the independent musician, who is most of the working population, nobody in the current arrangement is obliged to answer it at all. That is the open question, and a third paper is being written on it. It is not finished, so it is not summarized here.

Detection is probabilistic, contestable, and degrades as generative models improve, so its accuracy is a function of a race it is structurally set up to lose.

From the argument above

What would show this is wrong

The argument is falsifiable, and the conditions are stated rather than implied.

Three conditions

If detection accuracy stopped eroding as generative models improved, the central asymmetry would collapse and the case would go with it.

If signing at creation proved to cost session time that working musicians will not spend, the framework would be correct and useless, which in practice is the same as wrong.

If the unmatched-royalty pool shrank under conventional identifier work alone, the substrate claim would be unnecessary.

None of those has happened yet. All of them are things that could.

What it does not claim

A signature binds a claim to a key. It does not make the claim true, and a system that confuses the two is selling something it cannot deliver. Nothing here detects AI use, because no test returns human and no cryptographic record can attest to the absence of a tool that left no trace. Absence is not signable.

What a chain can show is what was recorded, by which key, at which moment, and where the record stops. Those are limits, not hedging, and a framework that hid them would fail its own standard on the first hard case.

Where to start

Three ways in

If you make records, start with the second essay, because the identifier layer is the part that decides whether your name survives the handoff.

If you hold a rights budget, start with the first, where the cost comparison between detection and signing is laid out in full.

If you work on standards, the papers on SSRN carry the formal versions and the citations.

Anyone arriving without a stake in any of that is better served by the map, then whichever question brought them here.
payload.title: On Provenance
